q: Which combination represents the conventional E. coli RNA polymerase core?
The core has two α chains plus one β, one β′ and one ω. A and D incorrectly include sigma in the core; C incorrectly substitutes a second β for β′.
Which core component is encoded by rpoC in E. coli?
rpoC encodes β′, including conserved catalytic metal-coordinating residues. rpoA, rpoB and rpoZ encode α, β and ω, respectively.
Why can a core enzyme extend RNA on a preassembled scaffold but fail to initiate efficiently at a natural promoter?
Sigma supplies promoter recognition and opening functions
RNA extension is independent of template sequence
A scaffold bypasses major initiation-specific requirements. Core retains RNA polymerization chemistry, so A is wrong; neither DNA polymerase nor template independence explains this result.
What defines a conventional bacterial RNA polymerase holoenzyme?
Core plus a promoter-specific sigma factor
Core plus two additional beta subunits
Holoenzyme is the core associated with an initiation sigma factor. A DNA primer is not required; the other options describe no canonical bacterial holoenzyme.
Which sequence is the familiar σ⁷⁰ −10 consensus on the nontemplate strand?
TATAAT is the classic −10 hexamer; TTGACA is the −35 consensus. AAUAAA is a common eukaryotic RNA processing signal, and AUG is a translation codon.
Which is the usual E. coli σ⁷⁰ −35 consensus?
TTGACA is the conventional −35 element. TATAAT is the −10 motif; the other choices do not represent this consensus, and AGGAGG resembles a bacterial ribosome-binding sequence.
What is the principal role of sigma region four in the classical σ⁷⁰ model?
Cleavage of RNA at a terminator
Region four recognizes the upstream −35 region. RNA cleavage, primer removal and translation are different molecular processes.
Which sigma region contributes prominently to recognition of −10 DNA and stabilization of exposed nontemplate bases?
Region two contributes to −10 recognition and DNA opening. Region four primarily contacts −35; ω and α support core organization rather than substituting for this sigma region.
Which pair correctly identifies the UP element's main RNA polymerase contact?
αCTD can contact upstream DNA directly. The other options confuse it with the −35 sigma interaction or unrelated molecular components.
A promoter with a weak −35 element remains functional because it has a favorable TG extension immediately upstream of −10. Which feature explains this?
An extended −10 can supply an additional sigma contact. Polyadenylation, replication origins and stop codons do not explain bacterial promoter recognition.
The last nucleotide of the −10 hexamer
The first nucleotide of the primary RNA
The final nucleotide at a terminator
+1 is the transcription start site, independent of translation start and termination. It is normally downstream of the familiar −10 element.
In a closed promoter complex, which description is best?
Polymerase has bound, but the initiation region is still base paired
A full RNA has been released
The promoter DNA has been excised
A ribosome is attached to RNA
The closed complex is promoter-bound without a mature melted region. The other choices describe later or entirely unrelated events.
Which property most directly distinguishes an open complex from a closed complex?
Local exposure of template bases near +1
An open complex has melted DNA in the start region. Both complexes contain DNA and core; sigma contacts can persist in the open state.
What supplies the immediate substrate energy for ordinary RNA chain extension?
A separate ATP molecule for every bond
Hydrolysis of a DNA phosphodiester bond
The triphosphate of the incoming NTP
The incoming NTP supplies the phosphate group and releases PPi. A separate ATP-driven motor is not obligatory for each addition; DNA cleavage and translation are not the source.
For conventional de novo initiation, which group is typically found at the 5′ end of the unprocessed primary RNA?
The initiating NTP normally retains its triphosphate. The 3′ hydroxyl is at the growing end; RNA has neither an amino terminus nor an obligatory DNA primer.
Which description of σ⁵⁴ initiation is correct?
It always uses the classical −35/−10 pair
Its closed complex ordinarily requires an ATP-driven activator for opening
It replaces the catalytic β′ subunit
σ⁵⁴ directs a distinct promoter class, typically −24/−12, and usually requires ATPase-mediated remodeling. The catalytic core remains present; this is transcription, not translation.
What is DNA scrunching during bacterial initiation?
Local accommodation of additional downstream DNA while upstream contacts persist
Scrunching accommodates additional DNA in a promoter-anchored initiation complex. It does not delete DNA, produce protein or establish replication forks.
Which product best exemplifies abortive initiation?
A full-length RNA released at its normal terminator
A short initial RNA released before productive escape
Abortive initiation releases a short nascent RNA before productive elongation. Normal termination and the unrelated DNA/protein products are not abortive events.
Which event is essential for promoter escape?
Disruption or reorganization of upstream promoter contacts
Cleavage of the promoter from DNA
Escape means the polymerase leaves its promoter-anchored initiation arrangement. Sigma can remain temporarily; DNA is not excised and termination follows elongation.
What does DNase I footprinting primarily report in a promoter-binding experiment?
The concentration of ATP inside living cells
The footprint reports differential cleavage accessibility. It cannot by itself measure protein mass, translation or cellular ATP concentration.
Which probe is commonly used to detect accessible thymine bases in melted promoter DNA?
Permanganate reactivity with exposed thymine provides evidence of local opening. The other choices do not serve this chemical probing role.
Why does an AT-rich −10 element not guarantee strong promoter activity?
Promoters are recognized only by ribosomes
Specific protein contacts, geometry and later initiation steps also matter
RNA polymerase copies only GC-rich DNA
AT richness can favor opening, but sequence-specific contacts and kinetics matter. The other options contradict the chemistry and biology of transcription.
What distinguishes archaea from the canonical bacterial sigma model?
Archaeal transcription generally employs factors related to eukaryotic basal machinery
Archaea possess multisubunit RNAP and distinct initiation machinery related to eukaryotic factors. They still synthesize RNA 5′ to 3′ and do not universally use bacterial sigma.
A sigma factor is named σ⁷⁰. What does 70 conventionally refer to?
The number of DNA bases contacted
The approximate molecular mass in kilodaltons
The length of the RNA at escape
Sigma names such as σ⁷⁰ reflect approximate molecular mass conventions. They are not counts of DNA bases, enzyme chains or RNA nucleotides.
Assertion: A promoter-bound polymerase need not be making RNA. Reason: Formation of an open complex and incorporation of NTPs are distinguishable steps.
Both true; reason does not explain assertion
Both statements are true and causally linked. Binding and opening can be observed before NTPs are supplied. The remaining choices incorrectly deny the causal separation.
Assertion: A σ⁷⁰ promoter with an exact −10 consensus may still be weak. Reason: Other contacts and kinetic transitions influence productive output.
Both true; reason does not explain assertion
The consensus represents one recognition element, not every determinant of flux. Spacing, opening and escape explain why exact motif matching need not yield high activity.

Assertion: Bacterial RNA polymerase needs no preexisting primer for ordinary de novo initiation. Reason: Its active center can position two initiating substrates to form the first phosphodiester bond.
Both true; reason does not explain assertion
The first NTP provides the attacking 3′ hydroxyl, so a separate preexisting primer is not needed. The reason explains the assertion.
Assertion: σ⁵⁴ commonly requires ATPase-dependent activation. Reason: Every σ⁷⁰ promoter must use a dedicated ATP-driven helicase.
Both true; reason does not explain assertion
The assertion is true, but the reason is false. Classical σ⁷⁰ opening normally uses holoenzyme–DNA interactions without an obligatory separate helicase.
Assertion: A mobility shift alone proves formation of an open complex. Reason: A DNA–protein association can alter electrophoretic mobility without DNA melting.
Both true; reason does not explain assertion
The reason is true and directly shows why the assertion is false. A binding assay cannot uniquely distinguish the closed and open states.
Assertion: Promoter escape and complete sigma dissociation are not identical events. Reason: Sigma can remain associated with some escaped elongation complexes.
Both true; reason does not explain assertion
Retention is documented and establishes that loss of promoter contacts need not require immediate full sigma release.
Select the true statements: I. Core contains two α chains. II. β and β′ are distinct subunits. III. Every holoenzyme contains σ⁷⁰. IV. Sigma helps promoter-specific initiation.
I, II and IV are correct. III is false because alternative sigma factors form holoenzymes with the same core.

Select the true statements: I. A consensus is a frequency-based summary. II. All promoters contain exact TTGACA. III. Spacer length can affect geometry. IV. Promoter orientation determines template selection.
I, III and IV are correct. II is false because the −35 element is variable and some promoters use compensating elements.

Which statements correctly distinguish experimental readouts? I. Mobility shift indicates association. II. Permanganate can report exposed thymine. III. Run-off RNA demonstrates product reaching a template end. IV. A footprint measures translation directly.
The first three describe distinct molecular observations. IV is false: DNA accessibility is not a translation measurement.

Which statements are valid? I. The incoming NTP supplies phosphate for an internucleotide linkage. II. An initial NTP can retain its 5′ triphosphate. III. Abortive RNAs use no NTPs. IV. Escape can depend on initially transcribed sequence.
I, II and IV are true. III is false because making a short abortive RNA also consumes nucleotide substrates.
Match 1. σ region 4; 2. αCTD; 3. σ region 2; 4. σ⁵⁴ with A. −10; B. UP; C. −24/−12; D. −35.
Region 4 recognizes −35, αCTD contacts UP, region 2 recognizes −10, and σ⁵⁴ recognizes the distinct −24/−12 class. Other mappings interchange distinct recognition functions.
Match 1. Closed complex; 2. Open complex; 3. Abortive initiation; 4. Escape with A. short RNA release; B. bound duplex; C. melted start region; D. loss of upstream initiation contacts.
Binding precedes opening, abortive initiation releases a short product, and escape reorganizes upstream contacts. The other mappings confuse the order or properties of the states.
A −35 hexamer occupies −35 through −30 and a −10 hexamer occupies −12 through −7. How many bases lie strictly between them?
The intervening coordinates are −29 through −13 inclusive: −13 − (−29) + 1 = 17. Twenty-three is the distance between motif starts, not the spacer length.
In ideal B-DNA with 10.5 bp per turn, a 3-bp spacer insertion changes relative phase by approximately how much?
The phase change is 3 × 360/10.5 ≈ 102.9°. The first two values correspond to one and two bases; 180° corresponds to about half a turn. Protein-bound DNA may deform.
At free holoenzyme 30 nM, two independent promoters have Kd values 10 nM and 90 nM. What are their equilibrium bound fractions?
Using θ = R/(R + Kd), the fractions are 30/40 = 0.75 and 30/120 = 0.25. The other choices reverse the affinities or use incorrect denominators. This is binding, not output.
At 310 K, an open-to-closed equilibrium ratio is 0.01. Using RT = 2.58 kJ/mol, calculate ΔG° for opening.
ΔG° = −RT ln K = −2.58 ln 0.01 ≈ +11.88 kJ/mol. A positive value agrees with the open state being less favorable; −11.88 reverses the sign.
A closed complex opens at 0.4 s⁻¹ or dissociates at 0.6 s⁻¹. What fraction opens first and what is the mean time to either event?
Probability = 0.4/(0.4 + 0.6) = 0.4; mean competing-event waiting time = 1/(0.4 + 0.6) = 1 s. Using only the opening rate gives 2.5 s, incorrectly ignoring dissociation.
An independent initiation attempt has productive probability 0.125; failures reset to the same bound state. What is the expected number of abortive attempts before a success?
Mean total attempts = 1/0.125 = 8, of which one is the productive attempt. The expected failed attempts are seven, not eight. The model assumes independent identical attempts.
A promoter makes a 120-nt run-off RNA and three 6-nt abortive RNAs, all by conventional de novo initiation. How many PPi molecules are released by polymerization?
The 120-nt RNA forms 119 bonds, and three 6-nt RNAs form 3 × 5 = 15 bonds. Total PPi = 134. Counting all 138 incorporated NTPs ignores the four initiating triphosphates.
For two competing sigma factors, free [S₁]/K₁ = 2 and [S₂]/K₂ = 5. Under the simple fixed-free-sigma model, what fraction of total core is bound to S₂?
The denominator includes free core: 1 + 2 + 5 = 8. The fraction for S₂ is 5/8. A denominator of seven excludes free core.
A hypothetical mutant gives binding 96%, opening 18% and full RNA 15% of wild type. Which interpretation is best?
A selective defect in opening is supported
It cannot bind DNA at all
The data prove a translation defect
Near-normal binding with sharply reduced opening supports a defect between recognition and opening. It does not uniquely identify the affected protein and says nothing directly about translation.
A mutant produces 94% normal open-complex signal but only 12% run-off RNA, with abundant short initial products and normal scaffold extension. What is the most likely affected stage?
Opening and scaffold extension are largely retained, while abortive output is high. This localizes the defect before stable elongation and after opening; replication and export are unrelated.
A sigma mutant restores activity on a particular altered −35 motif but loses activity on the original motif. Core abundance is unchanged. Which conclusion is best?
The mutant acquired altered promoter preference
The promoter is now a terminator
The sigma mutation changed the RNA genetic code
Selective reciprocal changes suggest altered recognition specificity. General catalytic failure would not selectively restore the altered promoter; termination and codon interpretation are separate.

Two promoters have identical −10/−35 elements. Replacing only promoter A's initially transcribed sequence with B's sequence changes the short-to-long RNA ratio without changing opening. What does this support?
The initially transcribed region can affect early RNA synthesis or escape
The DNA sequence no longer matters

The substitution changes a feature encountered after opening, consistent with altered short RNA stability or escape. Normal opening excludes complete loss of that transition; the data do not show one unique atomic mechanism.
An αCTD-defective RNAP and deletion of an UP element each strongly reduce promoter output. Combining the two changes has little further effect. What is the best interpretation?
They may disrupt the same functional interaction; a floor effect remains possible
The two proteins are proved identical
UP DNA is a translated codon
The result demonstrates zero binding at all promoters
Nonadditivity is consistent with both changes impairing αCTD–UP interaction, but measurement floors or other shared bottlenecks can mimic it. The other claims are not established.

An Eσ⁵⁴ complex binds promoter DNA in the absence of an activator, yet a probe shows little melting. Adding an ATPase-defective activator does not restore melting. Which step is most directly implicated?
ATP-driven remodeling of the closed complex
The intact binding step and failed opening point to activator-mediated remodeling. None of the other steps explains a promoter-bound, unmelted σ⁵⁴ complex.

A promoter gives a strong DNase I footprint but lacks a permanganate signal. The candidate melted interval contains several thymine bases, and the wild-type control gives a clear signal. Which conclusion is strongest?
It is certainly a mature elongation complex
DNA association occurs, but opening is impaired or below detection
Protection demonstrates altered accessibility and the comparative chemical signal supports impaired opening. The result does not exclude every possible open conformation or directly show elongation.
A protein reporter decreases fourfold after a change that also shifts +1 downstream. Direct run-off RNA yield stays similar. What is the best next interpretation?
A leader-dependent RNA stability or translation effect should be tested
The promoter lost all polymerase binding
Protein output is a direct measure of only k₁
A changed 5′ leader may influence RNA lifetime or translation while RNA synthesis remains similar. Reporter protein integrates several processes; it cannot alone quantify recruitment.
A long RNA band becomes twice as intense as a short band in a uniformly labeled nucleotide incorporation assay. What can be concluded about molecule numbers?
There are exactly twice as many long RNAs
The relative molecule count requires correction for label incorporation and detection
Short RNA molecules are never labeled
Signal depends on incorporation and detection, not necessarily one signal unit per molecule. Length and labeled nucleotide composition must be accounted for before estimating molecule ratios.
A DNA fragment bears an intact σ⁷⁰ consensus promoter, but insertion of eleven bases in its spacer nearly eliminates activity. Why is restored approximate helical phase insufficient?
The insertion also changes axial spacing and domain reach
The DNA no longer contains the consensus motifs
Eleven bases eliminate all DNA hydrogen bonding
One turn approximately restores rotational phase but increases axial separation. The two recognition regions may no longer fit the holoenzyme geometry despite unchanged motifs.

A single-molecule assay shows additional DNA unwinding as initial RNA length rises while upstream promoter contacts remain stationary; the signal reverses when short RNA is released. Which model best fits?
Entire polymerase translocates without additional unwinding
Additional unwinding with stationary upstream contacts is the prediction of scrunching; reversal upon abortive release fits reset. The alternatives do not account for the coupled DNA and RNA changes.

traps: Core versus holoenzyme
Core retains catalytic capacity; sigma enables effective specific promoter initiation. Core activity on an artificial substrate is not proof of normal initiation.
Consensus versus invariant sequence
TTGACA and TATAAT are statistical consensus motifs, not mandatory identical words at every bacterial promoter.
Spacer versus motif-start distance
For −35…−30 and −12…−7, the spacer contains 17 bases; motif starts are separated by 23 positions.
Upstream versus left
Upstream is defined relative to transcription direction, so it can be on either side of a chromosome drawing.
Start codon versus start site
+1 marks the first RNA nucleotide, while AUG usually marks the start of a translated reading frame.
Closed versus open complex
Binding does not prove melting. An open complex can exist without RNA synthesis when NTPs are absent.
AT content versus stability
Hydrogen bonds are only one contribution to duplex stability; stacking, topology and protein contacts also matter.
ATP as fuel versus substrate
σ⁵⁴ activator ATP hydrolysis is distinct from ATP incorporation as an RNA nucleotide; classical σ⁷⁰ opening lacks an obligatory separate ATP motor.
Affinity versus flux
A stable bound complex can be slow to open or escape. Occupancy is not productive initiation rate.
Short RNA versus termination
An abortive product is released before productive elongation; termination releases a transcript after elongation.
Escape versus sigma release
Escape entails disengaging initiation-specific promoter contacts. Sigma can remain associated in some elongation complexes.
RNA abundance versus transcription rate
Steady-state RNA depends on synthesis and loss, while protein reporter output also depends on translation and protein stability.
Bacteria versus all prokaryotes
Archaeal transcription machinery is not the bacterial α₂ββ′ω–sigma system.
Melted length versus RNA length
A representative open bubble includes upstream bases; its size is not the length of a nascent RNA.
Footprint versus bubble
Protection from nuclease cleavage indicates altered accessibility and is not a direct measurement of the number of melted base pairs.
recall: Why is sigma called a specificity factor?
It contributes promoter recognition and initiation-complex formation, allowing a common catalytic core to select different promoters.
What is the normal chain count of core and holoenzyme?
Five core chains, six with one sigma factor in the canonical E. coli model.
Which way does polymerase read DNA?
3′ to 5′ on the template; RNA grows 5′ to 3′.
What changes during open-complex formation?
Local DNA base pairing is disrupted and the strands are organized in distinct paths, exposing the template.
Why does σ⁵⁴ provide an exception to the σ⁷⁰ model?
Its closed complex ordinarily requires an ATP-driven activator to remodel it for opening.
What happens to the first NTP's 5′ phosphates?
They normally remain at the primary RNA 5′ end in conventional de novo initiation.
How does scrunching accommodate RNA growth?
The initiation complex retains upstream contacts while drawing additional downstream DNA into the enzyme.
How can a promoter mutation affect escape without altering RNA sequence?
It may change the strength or geometry of upstream contacts that must be disrupted.
What assay combination can separate binding from opening?
A mobility shift or footprint, combined with suitable chemical probing of exposed bases.
Why can increased promoter binding fail to raise full-length RNA?
Opening, nucleotide addition, abortive cycling or escape may remain limiting.
What does a run-off product reveal?
Successful RNA synthesis to the defined end of the linear template, not necessarily physiological termination.
What is the basic downstream hand-off?
The escaped complex contains polymerase, template DNA and nascent RNA ready for productive elongation.
checklist: I can reconstruct α₂ββ′ω and explain each subunit's contribution.
I can distinguish sigma-mediated specificity from polymerization chemistry.
I can orient a promoter and calculate its spacer correctly.
I can explain the −10, −35, extended −10, UP and discriminator features without treating them as universal requirements.
I can predict consequences of sigma or promoter mutations from multiple assays.
I can explain opening, de novo catalysis, scrunching, abortive initiation and escape in causal order.
I can distinguish σ⁷⁰ and σ⁵⁴ initiation and the roles of ATP.
I can apply the binding, competing-rate, abortive-cycle and RNA abundance models with their assumptions.
I can interpret footprinting, melting and RNA product measurements separately.
I can distinguish promoter clearance from immediate sigma dissociation and from termination.
